title: Amberley UFO sighting remains an enduring Ipswich mystery
excerpt: A 1973 Amberley sighting of unexplained lights remains a local mystery, set against the RAAF base’s rich aviation history.
content:
IPSWICH is accustomed to impressive aircraft overhead, but a strange light in the direction of RAAF Base Amberley can still send imaginations into orbit.

Is it a military aircraft, a helicopter – or a visitor whose navigation system has confused the Bremer River with the Milky Way?

The base provides the perfect setting for a UFO legend: powerful aircraft, restricted access and enough mystery beyond the gates to keep a good yarn airborne.

Yet behind the speculation about extraterrestrial visitors is a documented sighting that gives Amberley’s story something more substantial than a mate’s cousin claiming to have seen a flying saucer.

- Advertisement -

An official RAAF report records security guard D. B. Griffin seeing two lights while on duty at Amberley on May 2, 1973.

Investigators considered Army Kiowa helicopters a probable explanation – considerably less exciting than aliens checking out Australia’s defences, but rather easier to accommodate on the flight schedule.

A named observer, a specific date and an official record give the encounter a firm place in local history. They establish that a sighting was reported, however, rather than proving anything arrived from another planet.

Still, the location does much of the storytelling as the more colourful version imagines alien spacecraft monitoring Australian defence capabilities. It is an entertaining premise, although the cited Amberley account offers no evidence of extraterrestrial surveillance. Whatever was behind those lights, an intergalactic reconnaissance mission remains firmly in the realm of speculation.

Amberley’s real aviation history hardly needs embellishment as the base began operations on June 17, 1940, and welcomed F-4E Phantoms in September 1970. The first F-111s arrived in June 1973, just weeks after Griffin’s reported sighting, beginning an association that lasted until the fleet’s retirement in December 2010.

Those dates do not explain the May encounter, but they place it within a period of change in the aircraft associated with Amberley.

Official interest in UFO reports also extended well beyond Ipswich. The National Archives holds records of Australia’s investigations into unusual aerial sightings, preserving the reports and the efforts to explain them.

Amberley’s encounter belongs within that broader history of people looking up, seeing something unexpected and asking what it was.

That is where the local story finds its appeal: a security guard sees unfamiliar lights, investigators suggest helicopters, and the military setting leaves just enough room for a more adventurous retelling.
